clinicalPearls: SLC6A1 encodes GAT-1, the principal GABA transporter; heterozygous variants impair clearance of synaptic GABA and disturb the balance of phasic and tonic inhibition.
The classic phenotype is myoclonic-atonic epilepsy (Doose syndrome) with onset in early childhood, frequently after a period of normal development.
Absence seizures (typical and atypical), myoclonic, atonic (drop attacks) and generalised tonic-clonic seizures are all characteristic.
EEG typically shows generalised spike-and-wave with background slowing; photosensitivity may be seen.
Intellectual disability, autism spectrum features and language delay are common and often become apparent around the time seizures begin.
Most pathogenic variants are de novo missense or truncating changes acting through haploinsufficiency, with some misfolded proteins exerting a dominant-negative effect.
Broad-spectrum agents effective in generalised epilepsy (including valproate) are generally preferred, and behavioural or gait regression may accompany seizure onset.
Ataxia, tremor and fine-motor difficulty can coexist with the seizure disorder.
reference.pathophysiology: SLC6A1 on chromosome 3p25 encodes GAT-1 (GABA transporter type 1), a sodium- and chloride-dependent transporter expressed on presynaptic GABAergic terminals and astrocytes that reuptakes GABA from the synaptic cleft, terminating inhibitory neurotransmission and recycling the transmitter. Heterozygous loss-of-function or missense variants, usually arising de novo, cause haploinsufficiency, and several misfolded mutant subunits additionally trap wild-type protein in the endoplasmic reticulum to produce a dominant-negative effect. The resulting derangement of GABA reuptake dysregulates both phasic (synaptic) and tonic (extrasynaptic) inhibition, generating cortical network hyperexcitability and abnormal thalamocortical oscillations that manifest as generalised seizures (especially absence and myoclonic-atonic types) together with impaired neurodevelopment.
additionalDifferentials: Other GABAergic genetic generalised epilepsies (GABRG2, GABRA1, GABRB3)
Myoclonic-atonic epilepsy of other or unknown cause
additionalInvestigations: Epilepsy gene panel or exome sequencing including SLC6A1
Prolonged or video EEG to capture generalised spike-wave and seizure semiology
MRI brain (usually normal; excludes structural causes)
Paired CSF and plasma glucose if GLUT1 deficiency is considered (qualitative)
Chromosomal microarray if a copy-number variant is suspected
redFlags: Developmental regression or plateau coinciding with seizure onset
Non-convulsive status epilepticus (absence or atonic status) causing prolonged confusion or repeated falls
Frequent atonic drop attacks with injury risk
Emergence of new seizure types or marked EEG deterioration
reference.prognosis: Seizures often become more controllable after early childhood and may remit in some, but intellectual disability, autism and language impairment usually persist; overall outcome varies with seizure control and the degree of developmental involvement.
pitfalls: Misclassifying as idiopathic childhood absence epilepsy and missing the genetic developmental diagnosis
Aggravating generalised seizures with sodium-channel-blocking agents
Attributing developmental difficulties solely to seizures rather than the underlying genetic disorder
Using a normal MRI to wrongly exclude a genetic epileptic encephalopathy
management: Treat the absence, myoclonic and atonic seizures with broad-spectrum antiseizure medication such as valproate, ethosuximide, lamotrigine or benzodiazepines, avoiding sodium-channel blockers that may worsen generalised seizures
Consider ketogenic dietary therapy in drug-resistant cases
Provide neurodevelopmental and educational support for the intellectual disability and language delay
Arrange autism spectrum assessment and behavioural interventions
Offer physiotherapy for hypotonia and undertake regular EEG and developmental review
Offer genetic counselling for the usually de novo autosomal dominant variant with recurrence-risk discussion, within multidisciplinary paediatric neurology follow-up
